items_missed: No agenda statement at all — opened straight into the three-day quote. No roadmap, no 10-15 minute timeframe, no 'sound good?' confirmation.
No 'How are you today?' — went from 'thank you so much for picking up my call' directly into the estimate.

Never stated the hourly rate. She explained that weekdays are cheaper than Thursday-Friday-Saturday and quantified the ~$1,300 delta, but never gave the actual per-mover per-hour number on a $13,000+ job.
Never covered what's included — no gas, truck, taxes, wrap, pads, bands, tools. On a four-mover two-truck full pack this is the whole value story and it was skipped.
No disassembly/reassembly mention on a full-home pack and move.
No 'no hidden fees' pitch. The only 'no fees' statement was about rescheduling.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned — and this customer is receiving a crew that will stay overnight in a hotel and show up in Richardson on day three, which is exactly when knowing the mover matters.
No deposit never mentioned. On a $13,316-$13,700 booking this is the single strongest reason to say yes today and it was left on the table.

Clock mechanics not explained — never said the clock starts on site, never explained the 15-minute increments, and never addressed the obvious question of how the clock behaves across the 5.5-hour drive day and the hotel overnight.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent. The customer opened the door herself — 'so that could be less if it doesn't take the seven hours for packing' — and Nicole answered only 'that is correct.' No consolidation tips, no take-a-carload tip. Partial credit only for surfacing that billing is for actual time consumed.
Estimate variables incomplete — no stairs or access at the Richardson destination, no walk distance, no traffic on a 5-5.5 hour interstate drive, no assembly time.
Never verified the details back. No bolded-list explanation, no 'reply with any corrections,' no hours or callback number beyond 'just give us a call.'
Never used the customer's name once in a 9.6-minute call.

Let a badly garbled price go uncorrected. The customer said '$1.30067 million' and later 'this $13' and Nicole answered 'Yes, that is right' both times. The customer may have hung up without an accurate number.

Availability was not checked before agreeing to dates. She said 'Yeah, we can do that' twice, then reversed with 'Oh, no, actually I do apologize, we're actually closed on that specific day.' The customer ended up sequencing the three days herself and settling with 'maybe we have no choice.'
Insurance explanation gave the $2,000 No Worries figure but not the 60c/lb baseline, and only because the customer asked.
top_strength: The estimate construction itself was genuinely strong and specific. She laid out all three days in concrete terms — four movers and two trucks, seven to eight hours to pack, four and a half hours for pickup, a five to five and a half hour drive to Richardson with a hotel overnight, four hours to unload — and landed a tight budget range of $13,316 to $13,700 including travel and overnight fees. She also handled the sticker-shock question well: when the customer asked why the price moved off the earlier $12,380, Nicole immediately and clearly explained the weekday-versus-weekend rate tiers and confirmed a Thursday delivery would bring it back down. Her explanation of estimate risk was honest in both directions — it could go up only if there are items not visible on the video, and it could come down because billing is for time actually consumed.
coaching_note: Nicole, the highest-leverage fix is the Save Your Ass speech, and this call handed you the perfect opening. When she asked 'so that could be less if it doesn't take the seven hours for packing,' the answer was not 'that is correct' — it was 'Yes, and here is how you make that happen: anything you can consolidate before we arrive shortens the day. Get the kids' toys into bins, pull the photos off the walls, empty the loose items out of drawers, and take a carload of the small stuff yourself. Every one of those saves packing time and lowers your bill. Does that make sense?' On a time-and-materials job of this size that speech is worth real money to her and real efficiency to us. Second priority is the differentiator block — you never gave the hourly rate, what's included, no deposit, Meet Your Mover, or the On-Time Guarantee. On a $13,000 booking with a crew staying overnight, 'no deposit required' and 'you'll get an email with your mover's photo a few days before' are exactly what makes this feel safe. Third, and this one is a hygiene risk: the customer said the price back to you as '$1.30067 million' and you confirmed it. Always restate the real number in plain dollars and get it echoed correctly — 'so that's thirteen thousand three hundred, up to thirteen thousand seven hundred, does that match what you have?' And use her name; Noriko never heard it once.
phone_presence_notes: Polite with a warm close, but the customer's name was never used once and Nicole's responses collapsed into near-verbatim repetition — 'Yes, that is right' and 'That is correct' six-plus times — with no acknowledgment of the customer's confusion over the $1,300 price jump or her resigned 'maybe we have no choice.'
audio_review_reason: Score of 2 triggers the low-warmth review rule. Worth verifying against audio because Nicole's side of the transcript is also noticeably garbled ('we have a separate of, in three days', 'we will be only your small items into boxes'), so it is unclear how much of the flatness is delivery versus transcription quality.
